angle.selected_angle: Ottoman Double-Naming to Single Identity: How Naming Policy Shaped Modern Turkish Nationalism
angle.rationale: Shows institutional power over identity: Ottoman double-naming (Arabic + Turkish) declined to Turkish-only naming 13c-17c. Not linguistic evolution but administrative formalization. Demonstrates mechanism of nation-building through concrete archival evidence (Ottoman registries).

hook.primary_hook: When Ottomans Decided You Could Only Have One Name: How A Naming Policy Changed Turkish Identity Forever
hook.entry_point: Visual: Ottoman registry entry with two names (Arabic + Turkish) → later entry with one name. This shift IS the story.
hook.conflict: Pre-Ottoman origins uncertain, but Ottoman *transformation* is well-documented (5 ESTABLISHED claims in registries, 2 STRONGLY_SUPPORTED on administrative codification).

research_foundation.readiness_rationale: Completeness 0.93 is second-highest in 5-cluster research (after ATASÖZLERI 0.88). Strong Ottoman naming evidence (5 ESTABLISHED, 2 STRONGLY_SUPPORTED claims). Mixed verdicts on pre-Ottoman origins (8 PROBABLE, 1 CONTESTED) and causality mechanisms. D6 recommends CONDITIONAL READY with specific mechanism clarifications.
key_strengths: Ottoman naming conventions well-documented in administrative records
Shift from double-naming to Turkish-only naming clearly attested (13c-17c temporal range)
Connection to Turkish nationalism and modern nation-state identity clear
Source independence strong; low circular citation risk
major_gaps: Pre-Ottoman Arabic-naming adoption history unclear (earlier mechanism undocumented)
Causal explanation of naming decline: administrative policy vs. social/cultural preference (unclear agency)
Geographic variation: was transition uniform across Ottoman territories? (Regional variation data limited)
Post-Ottoman Turkish nationalist naming policies: extent of state enforcement vs. popular adoption (implementation gaps)
readiness_conditions: Condition 1: Acknowledge pre-Ottoman origins uncertainty — 'Before Ottoman administrative codification, naming practices are less clearly documented.'
Condition 2: Distinguish administrative vs. practice — 'Ottoman records show official naming conventions; actual population practice may have varied.'
Condition 3: Note causality qualification — 'Whether double-naming declined due to administrative policy, cultural preference, or both remains debated.'
Condition 4: Maintain administrative vs. practice distinction — 'Naming conventions in Ottoman records (ESTABLISHED) vs. actual naming practices among general population (PROBABLE).'

content_brief.target_audience: Ottoman history enthusiasts, Turkish nationalism scholars, identity/genealogy interest, general audience curious about naming and nation-building
content_brief.narrative_approach: Institutional/administrative documentation + genealogical/personal angle contrasted with policy-level change
content_brief.content_warnings: Mild geopolitical sensitivity on Turkish nationalism (non-controversial framing available; nationalism is historical fact, not ideology endorsement)

narrative_acts.title: Pre-Ottoman Islamic Naming Traditions (inferred)
narrative_acts.content: Arabic name adoption in Islamic period (mechanism unclear). Dual-naming tradition established. Note pre-Ottoman evidence is limited; narrative marks this as inference from later patterns.

narrative_acts.title: Ottoman Double-Naming Documented (13c-17c peak)
narrative_acts.content: Ottoman registries show Arabic + Turkish naming convention as standard practice. Museum examples, archival documents on screen showing two-name entries. Geographic distribution of double-naming practice across Ottoman territories.

narrative_acts.title: Administrative Codification & Turkification (16c-17c transition)
narrative_acts.content: Ottoman naming policy shift from multicultural cosmopolitanism (Arabic-Turkish synthesis) to Turkified identity (Turkish-only names). What drove this shift? Administrative reform, cultural preference, or both? Historians debate; evidence points to policy influence.

narrative_acts.title: Turkish Nationalism & Modern Naming Identity (20c onward)
narrative_acts.content: Modern Turkish nation-state inherited Turkified naming as marker of national identity. Turkish language reform context. Modern Turkish naming conventions as continuation of Ottoman Turkification trend.

production_scope.visual_style: Archival/institutional focus + genealogical documentation + comparative naming tables + administrative evolution
primary_visual_assets: Ottoman registry pages showing two-name entries (museum/archive photography)
Chronological comparison tables (frequency of double-naming over 13c-17c)
Geographic maps showing double-naming distribution across Ottoman territories
Ottoman administrative reform documents (tomar, naming policy directives if accessible)
Museum display of Ottoman naming registers
Modern Turkish naming conventions (modern registry examples for comparison)
Ottoman seals bearing personal names (muhrü examples)
Genealogical visualization (family trees showing name transitions across generations)
production_scope.interview_potential: Medium-High — Ottoman historians, Turkish nationalism scholars, genealogy/naming experts, Ottoman archive curators
production_scope.archival_material_available: High — Ottoman tomar (tax registers), naming registers, administrative correspondence

production_notes.historiographic_transparency_required: Yes — Causality debate (policy-driven vs. cultural preference) must be acknowledged without false resolution
production_notes.geopolitical_sensitivity: LOW-MEDIUM — Turkish nationalism is historical fact; framing available that is scholarly rather than ideological
caveats_detail: Pre-Ottoman uncertainty: 'Before Ottoman administrative codification (roughly 13c), naming practices are less clearly documented in available sources. Arabic-naming adoption likely occurred during Islamic period, but specific mechanisms remain unclear.'

Causality ambiguity: 'Ottoman records show that double-naming declined; what caused this decline — administrative policy, cultural preference for Turkified identity, or both — remains debated by scholars.'

Administrative vs. practice distinction: 'Naming conventions in Ottoman official records represent administrative standards; actual population naming practices may have varied, especially in non-Ottoman-era peripheral regions.'

Geographic variation: 'The transition from double-naming to Turkish-only naming may not have been uniform across all Ottoman territories. Regional variation likely but precise geographic data limited.'
